Since each $X_i$ has law $P$, applying the same measurable function to each gives a common law; [F10] preserves their mutual independence, so each resulting sequence is IID by [F2]. The fourth-moment hypothesis and [F8] make every product entry integrable, and [F9] identifies its expectation with the corresponding integral under $P$. Applying [F4] to these IID sequences gives $\bar h_n\to\theta$, $\bar f_n\to Pf$, $n^{-1}\sum_i h(X_i)h(X_i)^{\mathsf T}\to E_P[hh^{\mathsf T}]$, and $n^{-1}\sum_i h(X_i)f(X_i)\to E_P[hf]$ almost surely. The centered formulas therefore give $\widehat\Sigma_n\to\Sigma$ and $\widehat c_n\to c$ almost surely; positive definiteness of $\Sigma$ and continuity of determinant imply $\widehat\Sigma_n$ is eventually invertible almost surely. The fallback definition makes $\widehat\beta_n$ measurable: on the open nonsingular set the inverse entries are ratios of polynomial functions, and on its closed complement the value is constant.

Each scalar entry of $h$, $f$, $hh^{\mathsf T}$, and $hf$ has finite variance: for products, [F8] gives $E[h_j^2h_k^2]\le(Eh_j^4Eh_k^4)^{1/2}$ and $E[h_j^2f^2]\le(Eh_j^4Ef^4)^{1/2}$. Independence and [F6] make distinct centered sample entries have zero covariance, so each raw sample average has variance its population variance divided by $n$. With $a=M/\sqrt n$, [F5] bounds each entry's deviation probability by its variance divided by $M^2/n$; choosing $M$ large proves the $O_P(n^{-1/2})$ rates. Fixed $q$ makes the finite union of entrywise bounds joint. Centering changes the raw moments by products of sample-mean errors, which are $O_P(n^{-1})$; hence $\widehat\Sigma_n-\Sigma$ and $\widehat c_n-c$ are jointly $O_P(n^{-1/2})$.

On the event that $\widehat\Sigma_n$ is invertible, $\widehat\beta_n-\beta^*=\widehat\Sigma_n^{-1}[(\widehat c_n-c)-(\widehat\Sigma_n-\Sigma)\beta^*]$, since $c=\Sigma\beta^*$. Step 1.1 and the adjugate-over-determinant formula show that the inverse converges to $\Sigma^{-1}$ almost surely on the eventually nonsingular set; extending it by zero on the singular event gives an $O_P(1)$ matrix sequence. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose bounds for this inverse norm and for the bracket in step 2.1 after scaling by $\sqrt n$, with total failure probability less than $\varepsilon/2$. On their intersection the product is bounded after scaling by $\sqrt n$, so $\widehat\beta_n-\beta^*=O_P(n^{-1/2})$ there. The singular-event probability tends to zero by step 1.1; the fallback value $0$ therefore does not change this order in probability.

By [F1], subtracting the two estimators cancels $\bar f_n$ and leaves exactly $-(\widehat\beta_n-\beta^*)^{\mathsf T}(\bar h_n-\theta)$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose finite bounds for each factor after scaling by $\sqrt n$ so that the probability either bound fails is less than $\varepsilon/2$; on their intersection, Cauchy--Schwarz in $\mathbb R^q$ bounds $n$ times the absolute inner product by the product of those bounds. Thus the inner product is $O_P(n^{-1})$ by definition.
